Noted — **backoff plus circuit breaker**. That means the full-jitter loop above stays as-is, wrapped in a breaker that trips `OPEN` on sustained failure and fails fast until a half-open probe succeeds.

Two parameters to pin down when we implement: the trip threshold (I'd default to a 50% failure rate over a 20-request rolling window rather than a raw consecutive-failure count) and the `OPEN` duration before the half-open probe (30s). Worth noting the tradeoff you accepted: during the `OPEN` window, users whose upload would have succeeded get an immediate failure — so the client needs a distinct error state for "service degraded, try shortly" rather than showing a generic upload error.

sessions.title: Any Obsidian plugin that can render markdown style tables?
sessions.lastUserText: Any Obsidian plugin that can render markdown style tables?

last.text:
Obsidian renders markdown tables natively — reading view and Live Preview both do it, and since v1.5 Live Preview has a built-in table editor (row/column drag handles, add/delete buttons). So if you just want tables to *display*, no plugin needed.

If what you actually want is better authoring/rendering, the three worth installing:

| Plugin | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Advanced Tables** | The classic. Tab-to-navigate like a spreadsheet, auto-format/align on the fly, sort by column, formulas, CSV export. Best if you write tables by hand in the editor. |
| **Markdown Table Editor** | Visual spreadsheet-style panel over the table — add/delete/move rows and columns, sort, justify headers, and paste CSV/Excel/Sheets data in as markdown. Best if you'd rather not touch pipes at all. |
| **Excel to Markdown Table** | Single-purpose: paste from Excel/Sheets/Numbers and it lands as a formatted markdown table. |

Two others depending on what you're after:
- **Advanced Table Xt / Table Enhancer** — merged cells (colspan/rowspan), vertical headers, custom CSS. This is the one if plain markdown tables aren't expressive enough for you.
- **Dataview** — generates tables from queries over your notes rather than storing them as literal markdown.

My pick: Advanced Tables if you're comfortable in the editor, Markdown Table Editor if you want a GUI. They coexist fine.

If you meant something different by "markdown style" — e.g. rendering markdown tables *outside* Obsidian, or styling them to look a specific way — say the word and I'll point at the right thing.

Sources: [Markdown Table Editor](https://community.obsidian.md/plugins/markdown-table-editor), [Obsidian plugins tagged #table](https://www.obsidianstats.com/tags/table), [Best Obsidian Plugins for 2026](https://www.dsebastien.net/the-must-have-obsidian-plugins-for-2026/)

---

- Searched the current Obsidian plugin ecosystem for table rendering/editing plugins

sessions.lastUserText: I have a movement library now. Can we take one of the movements from a different clip and then try it again and see if it works? Or, take a…

last.text:
Recorded in both the repo README and project memory, since it's a durable platform constraint rather than a one-off.

**Where this leaves the pipeline — and it's better than it looked an hour ago:**

Motion control genuinely solves the problem that four models and six prompts couldn't. It produced a correct shoulder roll when nothing else would, because the form comes from a human instead of a model's prior. That result stands. The only constraint is on *whose* human.

So the production shape is now clear:

- **You film each movement once** — fifteen seconds, phone, any room, any lighting. It's a motion source, not a shot.
- **Motion control restyles it** onto the demonstrator in the bedroom or living room.
- **`make_loop.py` and `build_guide.py`** turn that into a looping guide with narration, which already works end to end.

And the movement library keeps its value — it's the reference for *what each movement is* and how it's cued, which is exactly what the segmented catalogues and READMEs were built for. You just perform them rather than sampling them.

Worth noting what this session cost to learn: today's spend is roughly 560 credits, and the four probes that settled the most important constraint cost nothing at all. The expensive part was the eleven text-driven renders that established these models can't do girdle rotation — which is real knowledge, but it's the thing motion control makes irrelevant.

Want me to write that shot list for filming the week-1 movements — framing, distance, what to wear, what to avoid, and which movements need which camera angle? It's the only thing standing between here and a working pipeline.

last.text:
**Live and verified:** https://eugenechantk.me/pages/fiftystrong-movement-library-69-movements-368b1f40/ (same URL as before)

## The canonical model is in

**73 canonical movements · 101 clips · 10 routines**

Sixteen movements now carry multiple clips, and the variant chips switch the video, keyframe grid, badge, position and source link in place:

- **Wrist & Forearm Stretch** — 5 clips
- **Spinal Twist**, **Spinal Full-Range Sequence** — 4 each
- **Cat-Cow**, **Shoulder Rotations**, **Side Bend** — 3 each

The dedup does exactly what you'd want: Spinal Full-Range Sequence is one entry showing standing *and* seated versions, rather than four cards you'd have to notice were the same thing.

New regions the added videos opened up: **Arms** (5), **Ankles & feet** (4), **Whole body** (2) — plus real strength content, which the stretch-only library didn't have.

## Two things went wrong, both worth recording

**I lost three source files.** Re-downloading at 1080p I used `--force-overwrites`; three failed their format selection *after* the flag had already deleted the 720p originals. Restored within minutes, but I should have downloaded to a temp name and swapped on success — which is what I did on the retry and every download since.

**The rep detector doesn't generalise to strength work, and I over-tuned trying to make it.** It was validated on stretches (9.0s, 12.2s, 38.25s all correct). Strength reps are 0.8–2s, below its 3-second floor. I tried three fixes — lower floor, monotone baseline, topographic prominence — and each gave a *different* answer while failing the known cases. My own protocol says that's the stop signal: when the answer moves every time, change approach or fall back to evidence.

So I stopped. Stretch videos keep the validated detector. Workout videos get a **"counted reps"** label and a 10-second clip showing several reps — honest, and for a library card it's actually better than a claimed period would be. That's now encoded as an explicit `REPS_FAMILY` in the code rather than a silent fudge.

## What's still outstanding

**Six videos not yet segmented** — the ones with no usable chapters, each needing the contact-sheet gate: standing abs, hip mobility, daily stretch, arm moves seated, stiff-neck routine, and the sit-down ab workout. Plus the 60-minute video's later sections (walking, balance, core cardio) — I took only its round-1 strength vocabulary, since rounds 2–3 repeat it and the canonical model makes those redundant anyway.

**Descriptions.** 73 canonical movements, and only 8 have the full setup/execution/hold/narration prose. That backlog is now much smaller than it would have been per-occurrence — which was the point of switching models.

I'd finish the six videos next so the library stops growing, then write descriptions in one pass by region. Writing them before the library settles means rewriting.

---
**Actions:**
- Downloaded 7 more videos at 1080p (16 sources total, 1.8 GB)
- Seeded, analysed and extracted 32 movements from 4 chapter-usable videos
- Diagnosed and stopped over-tuning the rep detector; added an explicit counted-reps fallback
- Built the canonical dedup layer: 101 occurrences → 73 movements, with in-card clip switching
- Rebuilt and redeployed; verified GET/HEAD/redirect/robots/byte-match and new assets

**Files:** `_reference/_lib/{canon,dissect,extract,library}.py` · `_reference/canonical.json` · `_reference/<slug>/` × 10 · `.claude/movement-library/site/` (48 MB)

last.text:
Albo is probably making around **$35K/month**, but this is estimated—not disclosed.

A defensible range is **$15K–$35K/month in App Store revenue**, or roughly **$180K–$420K annualized**:

- ScreensDesign currently shows **$35K/month and 65K monthly downloads**; an older snapshot on the same page shows $15K and 30K downloads. [ScreensDesign](https://screensdesign.com/showcase/albo-save-organise)
- Albo claims **250K+ users**. [Albo affiliate page](https://albo.inc/affiliate-program)
- Its main annual subscription is **$29.99**. [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/albo-save-organize/id6578421992)
- At $35K revenue and 65K downloads, the implied purchase rate is approximately **1.8%**, consistent with the older snapshot’s ratio.
- The company was only incorporated in February 2025, and its first accounts are not due until November 2026, so there are no public financials yet. [Companies House](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/16271351)

That is revenue, not profit. Payroll, AI extraction, infrastructure, App Store fees, and Albo’s 30% affiliate commission could consume much of it.

## Is link saving a good space?

**As a standalone category: mediocre. As an entry point into something more valuable: good.**

The core problem is genuine and widespread, but generic link storage has structural weaknesses:

- Browser bookmarks, Instagram/TikTok saves, Notion, and Apple Notes are free substitutes.
- People enjoy saving far more than revisiting, creating poor retention.
- Willingness to pay for “better storage” is limited.
- Social-content extraction is brittle when platforms change.
- AI processing creates variable costs.

The market can support strong indie businesses: mymind is estimated around **$880K ARR**, while Albo may be approaching a $400K annual revenue run rate. But Pocket shutting down despite having millions of users is an important warning: massive usage does not automatically create a sustainable business. [Mozilla’s Pocket announcement](https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/future-of-pocket)

My recommendation: **don’t build “another bookmark manager.”** Use saving as the capture mechanism, then monetize an outcome:

- Social recipes → meal planning and groceries
- Saved places → maps, itineraries and bookings
- Saved products → price tracking and affiliate commerce
- Saved knowledge → synthesis, creation and decision support

Albo itself appears to understand this: recent releases emphasize cook mode, grocery lists, maps, events, reviews, and social planning—not merely link storage.

**Verdict:** good space for a focused, profitable consumer app; questionable as a venture-scale category unless the saved-content graph becomes a transaction, creation, or social-discovery platform.

- Actions taken: Researched Albo’s users, pricing, estimated revenue, corporate filings, and competitive signals.
- Files changed: None.
- Verification: Cross-checked current app-intelligence estimates against pricing, download volume, Albo’s claims, App Store data, and Companies House.

sessions.lastUserText: Is it possible for an iPhone app to capture what app the person is using now? Maybe in the background, or when I press my app on the action…

last.id: 2026-08-14T10:34:05.311Z:message::No—not reliably through public App Store APIs.
last.text:
No—not reliably through public App Store APIs.

- **Normal app/background:** Your app cannot determine which other app is currently foregrounded. Background execution doesn’t grant this visibility.
- **Action Button / App Intent:** It can invoke your action from another app, but Apple doesn’t pass the previous app’s identity. [App Intents documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents)
- **Share Sheet:** This is the closest workable option. A Share Extension receives content the current app explicitly shares—URL, text, image, etc.—but the documented API doesn’t provide a reliable host-app bundle identifier. You can sometimes infer the service from a shared URL, such as `instagram.com`, but that isn’t guaranteed. [NSExtensionContext](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nsextensioncontext)
- **Screen Time APIs:** With Family Controls authorization and Apple-approved entitlements, you can obtain aggregate usage or threshold events—not a live “current app” feed. Standard access uses privacy-preserving app tokens. Apple’s newer non-tokenized access is EU-only, limited to one authorized app, and its smallest documented reporting segment is hourly. [Family Controls](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/familycontrols), [Device Activity](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/deviceactivity), [EU data access](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/familycontrols/authorizationstatus/approvedwithdataaccess)

My recommendation: build a Share Extension that records the timestamp and shared payload, then infer the source from its URL/content or ask for a one-tap confirmation. If you meant the hardware Action Button rather than the Share Sheet, automatic detection isn’t possible.

**Actions taken:** Checked current Apple APIs for App Intents, extensions, Family Controls, and Device Activity.  
**Files changed:** None.  
**Verification:** Confirmed against current Apple Developer documentation.

All six design screens are now built. **147 tests pass, lint clean, build green.**

**Profile** — http://localhost:3100/profile — renders her real quiz data: four dimension bars with the START HERE chip on her primary, then her five answers read back verbatim.

## The part that mattered most

The Profile shows her own words back to her, so **I extracted every question and option from the live quiz rather than writing them myself** — then added a test that asserts `measures.ts` text still appears in `quiz.ts`. If the quiz gets reworded, the build fails instead of quietly showing her an answer she never chose. That same wording is what the week-4 retest compares against, so it has to match on both sides.

## Three judgement calls, all reversible one-liners

**Scores round down, not to nearest.** Margaret's mobility averages 1.5 (effortful floor transfer, stiff in two areas). Rounded down it reads "Needs attention" rather than "Room to build". For a health product, meeting her at the lower level is the honest read — and it happens to match what the design shows.

**"I've never tried" scores level with "Not really"** on the one-leg test. An unknown isn't a worse result than a known difficulty; scoring it lowest would punish her for not having tested herself.

**The fourth segment is never filled.** Best case is 3 of 4. "You're already at the top" isn't a message this product should send in week one — the last segment is the headroom the programme exists for.

## Two things I fixed en route, and one to know about

I caught a real bug while verifying: **the bar length and the label could disagree** — I'd had segments as `score + 1` while the label used thresholds, so a "Room to build" showed three bars. Both now derive from `segmentsFor()`, and a test locks them together.

**Your database had two Margarets.** `pnpm seed` claims to be safe to re-run, but `display_name` has no unique constraint, so a second person was created at some point. I deleted the orphan (zero runs) and kept the one your cookie points at. The seed script's idempotency claim is still false — worth fixing before it bites on real data.

**`/programme` renders fine but is thinner than its data.** It shows period names and dots; it doesn't surface `week.title`, `week.summary`, `period.emphases`, or the "set from your week-4 check" line your programme doc explicitly asks for. That needs a design decision, not just code.

last.text:
Confirmed — the first is the old seed from earlier testing (0 linked quizzes), the second is from the purchase (1 linked). The replay created nothing.

**Storage and association are built and working end to end.** 143 tests, lint clean, build green.

## The identity that threads the funnel

One id, issued on her first answer, carried the whole way:

```
quiz first answer  →  publicId "rJTXs3NN_v4TGluD"  (localStorage + cookie)
                   →  /checkout?qid=rJTXs3NN_v4TGluD
purchase           →  createPersonFromQuiz(qid)
                   →  person + programme built from her emphasis
                   →  her personal link /s/<token>
```

It's a **correlation handle, not a credential** — it travels in URLs and localStorage, so it grants no access on its own. Her actual credential is still the `token` issued after purchase. That separation matters: otherwise anyone with a quiz link could read someone's account.

## Verified against the real quiz, not mocks

I clicked an actual option in the live quiz and watched it land in Postgres. Then I let the quiz's own scoring engine run on a realistic answer set — it produced `primary: balance`, `secondary: mobility`, `mode: confirm`, and all of it stored. Then the purchase call built a 12-week programme with `primaryEmphasis: balance`, matching what the quiz measured.

## Four decisions worth knowing

**Abandoned sittings are kept.** A row is created on her first answer, not at the end, and `pagehide` flushes via `sendBeacon`. An unfinished quiz is still the best record of who was interested and what they needed.

**Saves never destroy.** A later partial save can't wipe a profile an earlier one recorded — otherwise reloading the final screen would erase her scoring. Tested.

**Purchase is idempotent.** Payment webhooks fire twice; the replay returned the same person and the same token, and created nothing. Tested.

**`mode` is stored, not just the emphasis.** The quiz computes whether her stated goal *agrees* with what was measured (`confirm`), *conflicts* (`reconcile`), or she's already strong (`maintain`). That changes how her plan should be framed, so it's worth having.

## What's left

`POST /api/quiz` is public and unauthenticated by necessity — it's called before anyone is a customer. Right now it's rate-limited only by a 200-answer cap. Before this goes live it needs real rate limiting, or someone can fill the table.

And payment is still the missing piece. `createPersonFromQuiz()` is the seam — when Stripe lands, its webhook calls that one function with `qid` from the checkout metadata. Nothing else has to change.
